issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
Marcus is a 54-year-old combat pilot, still flying for a commercial airline, though every takeoff now feels like a rehearsal for disaster. The traumatic event happened eighteen months ago, during a routine training exercise over open ocean. A sudden mechanical failure in his fighter jet sent the aircraft into an unrecoverable spin, and for thirty-seven seconds—an eternity he has counted a thousand times—he was certain he was going to die. He ejected at the last possible moment, the canopy fracturing around him as the G-forces pressed him into his seat, and he remembers the strange silence after the parachute deployed, the water below him flat and gray, the wreckage of his plane already sinking. He was rescued within the hour, physically unharmed, but something inside him had already broken that he could not name.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus tried to return to normal life. He went back to work, sat through briefings, flew his commercial routes. But he found himself scanning the cockpit instruments obsessively, checking and rechecking systems he had trusted for decades. He had come to believe that the person who had survived that spin was not the same person who had entered it. He felt hollowed out, as if his capacity for normal emotion had been stripped away, and he would say to his wife, with genuine bewilderment, that he could not remember what it felt like to be happy or calm. He was certain that the accident had permanently damaged something essential in him, that he had changed for the worse and would never find his way back. What frightened him most was the sense that he no longer knew who he was—that the confident, decisive pilot he had been was gone, replaced by a stranger who was always watching, always waiting.

This sense of permanent damage began to shape every moment of his day. Because he felt fundamentally changed, broken in a way that could not be undone, he started to believe that danger was everywhere, that the world was now a place where catastrophe could strike without warning. He began planning escape routes everywhere he went—in the grocery store, in the airport terminal, even in his own living room. He would sit at the dinner table and find himself calculating the quickest path to the back door, his eyes moving from window to window, his body tense and ready. At home, he felt no relief. He was on guard even inside his own house, unable to relax, his sleep fractured by sudden starts and a constant low-level vigilance that exhausted him. He was hypervigilant in a way that his wife found alarming; she would touch his shoulder and he would flinch, his heart hammering, his mind already running through the nearest exit.

The cycle tightened over the months. The more he believed he was permanently damaged, the more he scanned for threats, and the more threats he found, the more damaged he felt. He stopped flying certain routes that passed over open water, claiming scheduling conflicts. He avoided conversations about the accident, deflecting with a tight smile. At work, his colleagues noticed he had grown distant, preoccupied, and his captain remarked that Marcus seemed to be flying by the book, rigid and joyless, as if he expected the plane to fail at any moment. His marriage suffered; his wife felt shut out, and he could not explain to her why he spent his evenings sitting in the dark, watching the street, or why he had started sleeping with his boots on.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment on the runway, his hands on the throttle, his heart racing so fast he thought he might pass out before the plane even left the ground. He had to call in sick, and he sat in the parking lot for an hour, staring at the terminal, knowing he could not do it again. He is terrified that he will never fly without fear, that the person he was is gone forever. But he is also, somewhere beneath the vigilance and the exhaustion, hoping that a part of that person might still be reachable.
